en: The attainment of urbanity (*nāgarikatā*) results from discerning the excellence of the illustrious through wit and being a connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*).
The excellence of young women and others resides in their body, their virtues, their ornaments, and their personal attendants.
In this context, the qualities that produce beauty are the *guṇas*.
1ab: Form, complexion, radiance, luster, noble birth, elegance, 1cd:
charm, the [major] marks, aura, and good fortune—these are the qualities.
The clarity of the lines of the parts is *rūpa* (form).
A specific quality such as whiteness is *varṇa* (color). [The form] consisting of glass and its objects... [Note: The source text appears to be truncated here.]
Luster (*kānti*) is like the brilliance of a gem;
radiance (*prabhā*) is the natural state of smiling, facial serenity, and so forth; and passion (*rāga*) is the quality that captivates the eyes of all.
*Abhijātya* (nobility) is a specific quality of touch characterized by softness and so forth, consisting of caresses and the like, which possesses the nature of a flower.

*Vilāsitā* (gracefulness) is a specific type of movement known as *vibhrama*, which brings about the manifestation of youth in the limbs and minor members, is impelled by the latent tendencies of the god of love, and is like a coquettish glance.

*Lāvaṇya* (loveliness) is a quality that, though its essence is the excellence of sweetness and smoothness—like nectar pervading the eyes and nourishing the surging, fluid nature—is like the full moon, providing delight and being manifested through the charm of physical form.

The defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the stable quality (*sthāyī dharma*) consisting of appropriateness (*aucitya*), which is the cause of the unique beauty and excellence of the primary and secondary limbs (*aṅga-upāṅga*).

Its [various forms] are known from: the possession of appropriate proportions; the absence of contact with defects; the smoothness of the face; the fixed density of the hair on the limbs; the well-knit joints; the appropriateness of height and circumference; and the presence of marks such as wheels and lotuses.

These are further categorized as: the perfection of limbs, the absence of defects, the quality of beauty, the appropriateness of proportions, and the possession of distinguished limbs not commonly found in the world.
In sequence, there are six varieties:
*chāyā* (luster) is a subtle grace manifested through refinement that reveals elegance in matters such as betel-chewing, attire, dancing, speech, and gait;

*saubhāgya* (charm) is the internal essence discernible through the fragrance and enjoyment of shimmering beauty, which acts as a magnet through its attractiveness and is perceived by those of sensitive taste.

In the former case, the varieties [of pleasure] consist of the horripilation caused by the intoxication of love and so forth; in the latter, however, because of the simultaneous possession of aesthetic flavor (*rasavattva*) through such means as moaning, the enjoyment of ornaments, the tasting of the lower lip, and fragrances, there is the attainment of the pleasures of the five senses.
Thus ends the first chapter, "The Description of Qualities," in the *Sahṛdayalīlā* composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Ruyyaka.
2ab: A jewel [is appropriate] for gold and silk garments, while a garland [is used] in the application of decorative substances.
2cd: "And miscellaneous"—these seven alone are considered by me to be the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
Among them, there are thirteen kinds of gems (*ratna*) in the form of diamond, pearl, ruby, emerald, sapphire, beryl, topaz, karketana, pulaka, bloodstone, *rudhirākṣa*, *bhīṣma*, crystal, and coral;
and gold is of nine kinds.

Gold is of four kinds, distinguished by its origin as *jāmbūnada*, *śātakaumbha*, *hāṭaka*, *vaiṇava*, *śṛṅgī*, *śuktija*, *jātarūpa*, *rasaviddha*, and *ākara-udgata*. It is further divided into four types according to its application: that which is to be pierced (*āvedhya*), that which is to be bound (*nibandhanīya*), that which is to be cast (*prakṣepya*), and that which is to be set in a setting (*āropya*).

In that regard, items such as the *tāḍī* leaf, earrings, and necklaces are to be pierced; items such as armlets, waist-bands, crest-jewels, and hair-pins are to be fastened; and items such as signets, bracelets, and anklets are to be slipped on.
Folded, twisted (or linked?), pillar-like, or like an anklet—
the *prālamba*, *mālikā*, *āhāra*, *nakṣatramālā*, and so forth, are to be arranged.
It is fourfold, consisting of [garments made from] fibers:
namely, those produced from bark, fruit, insects, and hair, distinguished respectively as *kṣauma* (linen), *kārpāsa* (cotton), *kauśeya* (silk), *rāṅkava* (wool), and so forth.
Furthermore, it is threefold:
This is due to the variety of what is to be fastened, what is to be inserted, and what is to be placed upon.
Among these, "to be fastened" refers to items such as the head-cloth and the lower garment;
"to be inserted" refers to items such as the bodice.
Having placed [it on the body], there are garments such as upper cloths (*uttarīya*) and so forth.
All of this is of many kinds due to the diversity of colors and patterns. Being twofold by virtue of being strung or unstrung, it is eightfold when consisting of garlands (*mālya*).

By way of the various types of garlands characterized by wreaths (*veṣṭita*), spread-out (*vitata*), joined (*saṃghāṭya*), knotted (*granthimat*), hanging (*avalamba*), loose (*muktaka*), anklets (*mañjīra*), and clusters (*stabaka*):
therein, that which is wound around is *udvartita*; that which is extended to the sides is *vitata*.
A *saṃghātya* is one fashioned from a multitude of many flowers;
it is uneven with knots here and there,
and clearly interwoven.
Avalambha;
it is exclusively independent,
a creeper consisting of many flowers, a cluster of blossoms.
A *kusumaguluccha* is a cluster of blossoms;
it has four varieties, beginning with the *āvedhya*.

It consists of decorative substances produced from musk, saffron, sandalwood, camphor, agallochum, *kulaka*, ivory, fragrant powders (*paṭavāsa*), mango oil, betel, lac-dye, collyrium, *gorocanā*, and so forth.
The art of arrangement (*yojanāmaya*) consists of joining the eyebrows, fashioning the curls, binding the braided hair (*dhammilla*), and so forth.
The art of scattering (*prakīrṇamaya*) is twofold,
distinguished by being performed for oneself or for one's bridegroom.
It is produced by fatigue, sweat, honey, intoxication, and so forth.
Items such as blades of *dūrvā* grass, *aśoka* sprouts, barley shoots, silver, tin, conch shells, palm leaves, ivory plaques, lotus stalks, bracelets, and hand-ornaments are to be employed.
The combination of these constitutes the costume (*veṣa*).
And that [beauty] is achieved through suitability regarding place, time, constitution, and state;
by the arrangement of these elements in their proper positions and the attainment of their relative aspects, there is an increase in loveliness.
Thus ends the second chapter, "The Description of Ornaments," in the *Sahṛdayalīlā* composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Ruyyaka.
The life-force known as youth (*yauvana*) is that which sustains beauty.

Following childhood, youth is a distinct stage of existence resembling a blossoming pomegranate; it is the abode of the God of Love, bestowing upon the limbs fullness, elegance, and distinct definition.
The transition between childhood and youth is its commencement,
while the middle stage is the period of maturity.

In the first [stage], there are the arranging of the braided hair, the styling of curls, the fastening of the lower garment, the cleaning and adorning of the teeth, looking into the mirror, gathering flowers, weaving garlands, water-sports, gambling, playful and clever speech, the manifestation of causeless modesty, and instruction in the arts of love.
These activities are revolving;
however, in the final stage, the gradation of the external manifestations (*anubhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is superior.
Thus ends the third chapter, "The Manifestation of Life," in the *Sahṛdayalīlā* composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Ruyyaka.
Regarding *śobhā* (beauty): because it is helpful from afar, its suggester (*vyañjaka*) is the *parikara* (the circumstantial).

Since that [suggester] consists of sentient and insentient beings, and of stationary and moving things, each of which exists in the form of either a pun (*śliṣṭa*) or mere proximity (*saṃnihita-mātra*), it is of eight kinds.
The sights include the lap, the attendant beloved, the horse, the retinue, the window, the canopy, the boat, the parasol, and so forth.
These are of two kinds,
according to the distinction between individual and collective.

Thus, the qualities (*guṇas*), ornaments (*alaṅkāras*), life-breath (*jīvita*), and the *parikara* (accessories) are, respectively, the producers of beauty, the illuminators, the vitalizers, and the manifestors.
In this way, because they assist one another, their mutual reinforcement is established.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the "Description of Accessories," in the *Sahṛdayalīlā* composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Ruyyaka.
This *Sahṛdayalīlā* is completed.
